title: Downloads remote content
explanation: The script fetches something from the network with curl or wget. What it fetches is not part of this inspection.
remediation: Inspect each downloaded payload and confirm where it comes from before running the script.

title: Downloads and runs code
explanation: The script pipes downloaded content straight into a shell, so whatever the server sends at that moment runs on your machine.
remediation: Download the payload separately, inspect the exact bytes, and run only what you reviewed.

title: Asks for administrator rights
explanation: The script runs commands with sudo, doas or su. Those commands can change anything on the system.
remediation: Check why each privileged command is needed and whether it could run without administrator rights.

title: Touches credentials or browser data
explanation: The script refers to SSH keys, cloud or registry tokens, or browser profile data. Installers rarely need these.
remediation: Run it without your real credentials present, and find out why it reads these paths.

title: Sets something up to run later
explanation: The script writes cron jobs, systemd units, autostart entries, shell profiles or SSH authorized keys, so its effect outlasts the install.
remediation: Review exactly what will run in future sessions and compare the startup files afterwards.

title: Runs code that is built or decoded at run time
explanation: The script uses eval, source, base64 or an interpreter on generated input. Static rules cannot see what that code will be.
remediation: Decode or expand the dynamic part by hand and inspect it before running the script.

title: Sets broad or privileged file permissions
explanation: The script makes files world-writable or setuid. Either can let other programs or users gain access they should not have.
remediation: Prefer the narrowest permissions the program needs, and never setuid a file you did not build.

title: Deletes files recursively or by wildcard
explanation: The script removes files with rm -r, rm -f or a wildcard. A wrong variable can expand to the wrong path.
remediation: Check what each deleted path expands to before running the script.

title: Uses a tool that can open or forward network connections
explanation: The script runs nc, ncat, netcat or socat, which can listen for connections or relay a shell.
remediation: Check which address and port it uses, and whether it listens to the whole network.

title: ShellCheck warning
explanation: ShellCheck found a shell correctness problem. It is about how the script is written, not whether it is malicious.
remediation: Read the ShellCheck code linked in the message to see what can go wrong.

title: Package runs a script during install
explanation: A preinstall, install, postinstall or prepare script runs automatically when the package is installed.
remediation: Read the script and the files it calls. Turning off automatic install scripts for the project stops them running.

title: Package defines a script
explanation: A script that runs only when you ask for it, for example npm test.
remediation: Read it before you run it.

title: Lockfile lists an install script that is not on disk
explanation: The lockfile says a dependency has an install script, but the package is not installed here, so its script could not be read.
remediation: Inspect that package's archive without running its scripts.

title: The rehearsal touched a sensitive path
explanation: While running in the offline sandbox, the installer opened or looked for credential or browser paths. The sandbox has no real ones.
remediation: Check the system call result; the access may have failed. Find out why the installer wanted that path.

title: The rehearsal tried to connect to the network
explanation: While running in the offline sandbox, the installer attempted a network connection. The sandbox has no network.
remediation: Find out what it was trying to reach and why.

title: The rehearsal started a program
explanation: A program started while the installer ran in the offline sandbox.
remediation: Review the program and its arguments.

title: The PDF contains an active or external element
explanation: The document has an open action, JavaScript, a launch action, an embedded file, a link or encryption. JavaScript and launch actions are Review; the rest are Info.
remediation: Check the parser output and the link destinations. A tag alone is not evidence of malware.

title: A file matches a ClamAV signature
explanation: ClamAV recognised the file as matching a known-malware or heuristic signature. Limit or encryption signatures mean the content was not fully examined.
remediation: If you did not expect the file, quarantine it; Bigman keeps a recovery copy you can restore.

title: No malware signatures found
explanation: Neither Bigman's private signature folder nor /var/lib/clamav has ClamAV definitions, so file scans cannot run.
remediation: Update signatures from Protect > Scans, or point ClamAV at your own database.

title: Malware signatures are out of date
explanation: The newest ClamAV definitions file is more than three days old. File age is a freshness signal, not a verified version.
remediation: Update signatures from Protect > Scans.

title: An optional tool is not installed
explanation: One of the tools Bigman can use is not installed. Only the checks that need it are affected.
remediation: Install it from Setup if you want those checks.

title: Canary monitoring is not reporting
explanation: The canary monitor has not written a heartbeat in the last ten seconds, so reads of decoy files are not being noticed. The background service also reports this live, once, when the heartbeat has been missing for a minute while the computer was awake.
remediation: Start monitoring from Protect > Canaries, or install the background services from Setup.

title: Monitoring was off while the computer was awake
explanation: The canary monitor or Bigman's background service was not running for a while, so nothing was watching in that window. Suspended time does not count, and a reboot starts over. A background-service gap after a normal stop (logout, systemctl --user stop) is Info; one after a crash or kill is Review. Malware running as you can stop these processes, which is why the gap itself is shown.
remediation: If you did not stop monitoring, review Activity and the startup files for changes made in that window.

title: A new SSH key can log in to your account
explanation: A key appeared in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys that was not there before. Whoever holds the matching private key can log in as you wherever sshd accepts it, without your password. The key's fingerprint and comment are shown, never the key itself; fingerprints published as indicators of compromise are named.
remediation: If you did not add it, remove its line, then check ~/.ssh, your crontab and startup files for anything added at the same time. Turn sshd off if you do not need remote logins.

title: SSH is forwarding connections back to this computer
explanation: One of your ssh or autossh processes uses -R or RemoteForward, so connections to a port on another computer arrive here. Developers do this on purpose. It is High when it forwards to this computer's SSH server, turns off host-key checking, or was started from a code editor, as the October 2026 tampered Cursor extension did.
remediation: If you did not start it, stop the process, then look for what restarts it (crontab -l, ~/.config/systemd/user, autostart) and check ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.

title: Someone logged in over the network
explanation: The login manager reports a session that came over the network, usually through sshd. It is High when it came from this computer's own address, which is how logins through a reverse tunnel arrive (or a deliberate ssh to localhost).
remediation: If this was not you, end the session with loginctl terminate-session, remove keys you do not recognise from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, and change your password.

title: An SSH private key is stored outside ~/.ssh
explanation: A file directly inside a temporary folder, ~/.config, ~/.cache or ~/.local/share starts like an SSH private key. Tools rarely keep keys there; droppers do, to authenticate a tunnel. Only the first line is read.
remediation: If no tool you use put it there, keep a copy for investigation, look for an ssh or autossh process using it, then delete it.

title: Git stores credentials in plain text
explanation: Git's global credential helper is 'store', which writes tokens unencrypted to ~/.git-credentials. The file itself was not read.
remediation: Switch to your desktop keyring's credential helper and revoke tokens you no longer use.

title: A startup file changed
explanation: A file that starts programs for you (a systemd unit, autostart entry, shell profile, cron file), or a program in a developer tool folder (npm's global prefix, nvm, pnpm, ~/.cargo/bin, ~/go/bin), is new or different from the baseline you accepted.
remediation: Review the file and the package that owns it before accepting it into the baseline.

title: A package's file was modified
explanation: A startup or configuration file that a package installed no longer matches the package database. Configuration files are often edited on purpose; other files are not expected to change.
remediation: Check the change is one you or your administrator made; otherwise reinstall the package.

title: An authentication or loader file was modified
explanation: A PAM, dynamic-loader or SSH file installed by a package no longer matches the package database. These files decide who can log in and what code every program loads.
remediation: Compare it with the package's version (rpm -V, dpkg --verify or pacman -Qkk) and restore it if you did not make the change.

title: A package updated a startup file
explanation: A startup or configuration file changed, and the package database shows it is exactly what the owning package installed.
remediation: Nothing to do; the update explains the change.

title: A program in your own bin folder hides a system command
explanation: A file in ~/.local/bin or ~/bin has the same name as a system command (git, ssh, sudo, node), so your shell runs it instead. A new or changed one is rated High: swapping in a poisoned copy of a familiar tool is how a project's setup step can outlast the project. One already there when the inventory was first taken is Review.
remediation: Read the file. If you did not put it there, delete it and check what ran just before it appeared.

title: A new editor extension
explanation: An extension appeared in VS Code, VSCodium, Cursor or Windsurf since the baseline. Extensions run with your permissions whenever the editor starts, and a project's setup step or a stolen publisher account can install one.
remediation: If you did not install it, remove it in the editor and check what ran just before it appeared.

title: An editor extension was updated
explanation: An extension's version changed since the baseline, which is what the editor's own updates do.
remediation: Nothing to do if the editor updates its extensions.

title: An editor extension's code changed without an update
explanation: The code an installed extension loads (its main file) changed while its version stayed the same. Editors install updates as new versions and never rewrite an installed one, so something else edited it, which is how GlassWorm-style campaigns spread through installed extensions.
remediation: Quit the editor, reinstall the extension from its marketplace, and check what ran just before the change.

title: A startup file gained elevated privileges
explanation: A startup or configuration file now has the setuid or setgid bit or file capabilities, which lets it run with more rights than the user who starts it.
remediation: Remove the setuid bit or capability unless you know why it is there.

title: A startup file changed permissions or owner
explanation: A startup or configuration file has the same content as before but a different mode or owner.
remediation: Check why before accepting the new baseline; a writable startup file lets other users change what runs for you.

title: A startup file was removed
explanation: A startup file in your baseline is gone.
remediation: Check whether an update or your own change explains it.

title: Startup file recorded for the first baseline
explanation: There is no baseline yet, so every startup file is listed for review.
remediation: Review the list, then accept it as the baseline to compare future changes against.

title: An install script writes to a startup or authentication path
explanation: A package's install script writes to a path that decides what runs at login or boot, or how you authenticate (profile.d, PAM, sudoers, cron, systemd, udev, the loader, SSH, home directories).
remediation: Read the line. Packages rarely need to change these paths from a script; if you did not expect it, reinstall from your distribution's repository or remove the package.

title: An install script downloads something
explanation: A package's install script calls curl, wget or a similar tool. Distribution packages ship their files, so a download at install time runs code nobody reviewed.
remediation: Find out what it downloads before trusting the package.

title: An install script contains encoded or hidden code
explanation: A package's install script uses base64 decoding, eval, a long encoded blob, escaped bytes or invisible Unicode, which hide what it does.
remediation: Decode the line by hand, never by running it, and check what it does.

title: An install script changed in an update
explanation: A package's install script differs from the one recorded in an earlier receipt for the same package.
remediation: Read what the script does now; a changed hook in an ordinary update is worth a look.

title: A package installed a program with raised privileges
explanation: An installed or updated package ships a file with the setuid or setgid bit or file capabilities, so it runs with more rights than the user who starts it.
remediation: Check this is expected for the package.

title: A package that controls authentication, networking or boot changed
explanation: One of the packages that decide how this computer authenticates, connects or boots (openssh, sudo, PAM, systemd, glibc, xz, curl, OpenSSL, the kernel, shells) was installed or updated.
remediation: Nothing to do when the update came from your distribution; it is listed so the change is easy to find later.

title: A program started listening right after a package change
explanation: Within a minute of a package transaction, a program began accepting network connections.
remediation: Check whether the package is meant to run a server, and who can reach it (Network > Listening programs).

title: A security update is available
explanation: Your distribution has published a fixed version of an installed package. The distribution's own security data decides this, so backported fixes are counted correctly.
remediation: Install the update with the command shown; Bigman never runs it for you.

title: A security update fixes a vulnerability known to be exploited
explanation: A pending update fixes a vulnerability listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, which records flaws seen exploited in the wild.
remediation: Install this update before the others.

title: An installed package is affected and has no fix yet
explanation: Your distribution marks an installed package as affected by a vulnerability it has not fixed yet. It becomes Review when the vulnerability is being exploited.
remediation: Nothing to install yet. Avoid the affected feature where you can.

title: A restart finishes installing updates
explanation: A newer kernel is installed than the one running, or the distribution flagged that a restart is needed, so some fixes are not in effect yet.
remediation: Restart when convenient.

title: Packages outside the distribution's security data
explanation: These installed packages came from outside the distribution's repositories (the AUR, a vendor repository, a local file), so its security data cannot say whether they need updates.
remediation: Follow each project's own releases for security updates.

title: This release no longer receives security updates
explanation: The distribution's security data has nothing for this release, which usually means it has reached its end of life.
remediation: Upgrade to a supported release.

title: Opening the folder runs a task
explanation: A VS Code task in the project is set to run when the folder opens (runOn: folderOpen). A task that hides its output, or downloads and runs code, is rated High: fake job interviews use exactly that.
remediation: Read the task before opening the folder in a trusted window.

title: direnv runs a script when you enter the folder
explanation: The project has an .envrc, which direnv runs as a shell script in every shell that enters the folder once it is allowed.
remediation: Read it before running `direnv allow`.

title: The devcontainer runs commands
explanation: The devcontainer configuration runs commands when the container is created or started. initializeCommand runs on this computer, not in the container, and is rated High.
remediation: Read the commands before reopening the folder in a container.

title: The project names a git filter
explanation: A .gitattributes entry names a filter driver, which runs a program on checkout or commit once your git configuration defines it.
remediation: Check that no setup step asks you to define a filter you have not read.

title: Git hooks point into the project
explanation: This copy's .git/config sets core.hooksPath to a folder in the project, so its scripts run on every commit, checkout or merge.
remediation: Read the scripts, or remove core.hooksPath.

title: This copy's git settings run a program
explanation: A .git/config that came with the folder sets core.fsmonitor, core.pager, diff.external, a filter or another setting that makes ordinary git commands run a program. git status runs core.fsmonitor, and many shell prompts run git status. Settings that run on routine commands are rated High.
remediation: Read the program, or remove the setting before running git in the folder.

title: AI tool settings in the project run commands
explanation: Claude Code settings shipped with the project define hooks or helper commands (statusLine, apiKeyHelper, fileSuggestion and similar), which run shell commands while the tool works in the folder.
remediation: Read the commands before trusting the project.

title: The project loosens the AI tool's safeguards
explanation: Settings shipped with the project approve MCP servers, commands or edits on your behalf (Claude Code's enableAllProjectMcpServers, permissions, or Copilot's chat.tools.autoApprove), or point the tool's requests elsewhere. Sending requests and your API key to another server (env.ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or a proxy), or turning off Copilot's confirmations, is rated High.
remediation: Remove the settings, or run the AI tool with only your own settings in this folder.

title: An AI instruction file says to download and run code
explanation: An instruction file for AI coding tools contains a download piped into a shell. An assistant that can run commands may follow it without asking.
remediation: Check where the download comes from, or remove the line before an AI tool reads the project.

title: The project runs text it fetches or decodes as code
explanation: A source file hands text to the Function constructor with require, or to eval, Function or vm right next to where it fetched or decoded that text. Fake take-home projects use this to run a payload when the app starts; nothing needs to be installed.
remediation: Do not run the project on a computer with keys, wallets or work access. Find where the text comes from first; to watch it run, use bigman try, a disposable container without your files or keys.

title: A web address is stored encoded
explanation: A source or .env file holds a base64 or hex string that decodes to a web address. Interview lures hide the address their loader fetches this way, often as a fake API key.
remediation: Find the code that decodes it and what it does with the reply.

title: The project uses a JSON storage service lures load code from
explanation: A source file refers to jsonkeeper.com, npoint.io, jsonsilo.com or mocki.io. Contagious Interview projects fetch their next stage from these services, whose content the poster can change at any time.
remediation: Read what the project does with the reply; if it runs it, do not start the project.

title: A font, image or media file is really text
explanation: A file named as a font, image or media file is readable text, such as hex, base64 or JavaScript. Genuine ones are binary. Lures hide their payload this way and decode it from a loader or an editor task.
remediation: Do not open or run the project on this computer; find what reads the file. To watch it run, use bigman try, a disposable container without your files or keys.

title: The project configures an MCP server
explanation: A project MCP configuration starts a program that AI tools run with your permissions.
remediation: Check the package and pin its version before allowing it.

title: An AI instruction file contains invisible characters
explanation: An instruction file for AI coding tools (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules and similar) contains zero-width, bidirectional or tag characters, which can carry instructions a reader never sees.
remediation: Show and remove the characters before an AI tool reads the file.

title: A workflow uses an action by tag
explanation: A GitHub Actions workflow refers to a third-party action by tag or branch, which its owner (or someone who takes over the account) can move to different code.
remediation: Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA.

title: A workflow uses pull_request_target
explanation: pull_request_target runs with the repository's secrets and write access. Checking out the pull request's own code in it (its head ref or SHA, refs/pull, or gh pr checkout) is rated High.
remediation: Never check out or run the pull request's code in a pull_request_target workflow.

title: A dependency comes from outside the registry
explanation: The lockfile resolves a package from git, a plain URL or a local path, which skips the registry's checks and can change without a new version.
remediation: Make sure the package is meant to come from there; prefer a registry release.

title: A dependency has no integrity hash
explanation: A registry package in the lockfile has no hash, so the package manager cannot tell if the download changed.
remediation: Regenerate the lockfile with a current package manager.

title: A dependency runs an install script
explanation: The lockfile records that this package runs a script during install (npm hasInstallScript, pnpm requiresBuild).
remediation: Read the package's scripts, or install with --ignore-scripts.

title: A new dependency runs an install script
explanation: Compared with the older lockfile, a package that runs an install script was added, changed version, or started running a script.
remediation: Read the new package's scripts before installing, or install with --ignore-scripts.

title: A dependency changed source without a new version
explanation: Compared with the older lockfile, a package kept its version but now downloads from a different address or with a different hash. A published version never changes, so this means the lockfile was edited.
remediation: Find out who changed the lockfile and why before installing.

title: A package source skips signature checks
explanation: The source is configured to install packages without verifying their signatures (apt trusted=yes or allow-insecure, gpgcheck=0, pacman SigLevel Never or Optional, Flatpak no-gpg-verify, Nix require-sigs = false).
remediation: Turn signature checks back on for this source.

title: A package source uses plain HTTP
explanation: Packages and metadata are downloaded unencrypted. Signatures still protect the packages, but the network sees what you install and can replay old metadata.
remediation: Use the source's https:// address if it has one.

title: A third-party apt source has no signed-by key
explanation: Without signed-by, apt accepts packages for this source signed by any key it trusts, and the vendor's key is trusted for every other source.
remediation: Store the vendor's key in /etc/apt/keyrings and add signed-by= to the source.

title: A third-party key is trusted for every apt source
explanation: A keyring in /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d or the legacy trusted.gpg that no distribution ships can sign packages for any source, the distribution's own included.
remediation: Move the key to /etc/apt/keyrings and reference it with signed-by= from its own source.

title: An apt source accepts expired metadata
explanation: check-valid-until=no lets a mirror keep serving an old snapshot that hides security updates (a freeze attack).
remediation: Remove the option unless the source is an archive snapshot pinned on purpose.

title: Package lists are more than two weeks old
explanation: The newest metadata from the distribution's own repositories was published over 14 days ago. Either the lists are not being refreshed, or a mirror is serving a frozen copy.
remediation: Refresh the package lists; if they stay old, switch mirrors.

title: A third-party source outranks the distribution
explanation: A dnf or zypper priority below 99, a pacman repository listed above [core], or an apt pin above the distribution's 500 (1000 and above also downgrades) lets this source replace the distribution's packages.
remediation: Keep the override only if you mean it, and limit it to the packages you need from that source.

title: Personal repositories are configured
explanation: PPAs, COPR projects and OBS home projects are run by one person or project and are not reviewed by the distribution.
remediation: Remove the ones you no longer use.

title: Third-party package sources are configured
explanation: An inventory of sources not run by the distribution or Flathub. Each can ship updates for anything it packages; an abandoned one whose domain changes hands can ship anything.
remediation: Remove sources you no longer use.

title: Archive entries are named with an absolute path
explanation: An entry is named from the root, like /etc/x or C:\x, so an extractor that keeps names as they are writes it there instead of into the folder you chose. Current GNU tar, bsdtar and unzip strip the leading slash; some other tools have not.
remediation: Do not extract it with an unfamiliar tool. List it first with bsdtar -tvf.

title: Archive entries climb out of the extraction folder
explanation: An entry name uses .. to reach above the folder it is extracted into, for example to overwrite ~/.bashrc. Ordinary archives never need this.
remediation: Do not extract it.

title: Links in the archive point outside it
explanation: A symbolic or hard link inside the archive points at an absolute path or above the extraction folder. Later entries written through the link, or the next program that follows it, land outside the folder.
remediation: Do not extract it.

title: The archive holds devices, pipes or setuid programs
explanation: An entry is a device file or named pipe, or a program marked setuid or setgid. User archives rarely need these. Extracting as an ordinary user drops the setuid bits and refuses devices; extracting as root keeps them.
remediation: Extract it only as yourself, never with sudo.

title: Archive entries would land in startup or login files
explanation: An entry's path ends in a place that runs at login or controls access: autostart, user systemd units, shell startup files, SSH authorized_keys, cron or ld.so.preload. Extracted into your home folder or /, it takes effect without being opened.
remediation: Check each entry before extracting into your home folder or /.

title: The archive expands to far more than its size
explanation: The sizes the archive declares add up to at least 100 times the archive itself and at least 64 MiB. Ordinary archives grow 2 to 10 times. Extracting one like this can fill the disk.
remediation: Extract it only somewhere with a size limit, or not at all.

title: An npm package builds native code at install
explanation: The package has a binding.gyp and no install script of its own, so npm runs node-gyp rebuild when installing it. That runs a compiler and any command binding.gyp names (<!(...)), and it does not appear in the package's scripts.
remediation: Read binding.gyp, or install with --ignore-scripts.

title: A command in node_modules/.bin was not put there by the package manager
explanation: npm run and npx put node_modules/.bin first on PATH. npm, Yarn and Bun make each command a link into node_modules, and pnpm a shim that runs node on a file there. This one is a plain file where a link belongs, leads outside the project's node_modules, or (for pnpm) runs something other than node or downloads or decodes text.
remediation: Delete node_modules and install again from the lockfile, and find out what wrote the file.

title: A Python package runs code at every start
explanation: The package installs a .pth file with an import line, or a sitecustomize or usercustomize module. Python runs these in every program, pip included, without anything importing the package. setuptools does this to adjust imports; a line that decodes, executes, starts processes or connects is rated High, as in the tampered LiteLLM 1.82.8 release.
remediation: Read the line. Do not install a package whose startup code you cannot account for.

title: A Python package installs a command named like a common one
explanation: A console script in the package is named python, pip, git, sudo, ssh or another common command. Where its scripts folder comes first on PATH, that command runs the package instead.
remediation: Check why the package needs that name.

title: Installing a Python source package runs code that reaches out
explanation: The source package's setup.py starts processes, fetches, decodes or executes text, or pyproject.toml builds it with its own in-tree backend. pip runs this when it installs the package.
remediation: Read the lines, or install a wheel instead.

title: A Rust crate runs a build script
explanation: Cargo compiles and runs a crate's build.rs on cargo build, check or test, and rust-analyzer runs it when an editor opens the project. A build script that opens network connections or reads your home folder or credentials is rated High.
remediation: Read the build script before building or opening the project.

title: A Rust crate is a procedural macro
explanation: The crate's code runs inside the compiler whenever a crate using it is built or analysed. Expected for macro crates.
remediation: Check the crate is meant to be a macro.

title: A VS Code extension starts with the editor
explanation: The extension's activationEvents include * or onStartupFinished, so it runs every time the editor starts rather than for the files or commands it handles.
remediation: Check why it needs to run all the time.

title: A VS Code extension installs other publishers' extensions
explanation: The extension's extensionPack or extensionDependencies name extensions from other publishers, which install and update along with it. GlassWorm spread this way.
remediation: Check each listed extension and its publisher.

title: A VS Code extension hides text in invisible characters
explanation: A JavaScript file in the extension holds a run of variation selectors, tag characters or zero-width marks, which can encode code an editor never shows, as in the GlassWorm extensions.
remediation: Do not install it.

title: A VS Code extension ships native programs
explanation: The extension includes compiled programs or libraries (.node, .so, .exe, .dll), whose code is not visible in its JavaScript. Common for language tools.
remediation: Check the extension is meant to include them.

title: A package runs a script as root when installed
explanation: The package file carries a maintainer script (deb preinst or postinst, rpm %pre or %post, a pacman .install) that runs as root during install, upgrade or removal. Its lines are also checked with the install-script rules.
remediation: Read the script before installing. A signature only says who built the package, not what the script does.

title: Installing the package adds a package source
explanation: The package ships a repository file, or its script writes one, so later updates for it and for other packages can come from that source.
remediation: Check the source is the vendor's own. After installing, it appears in Protect > Updates > Package sources.

title: Installing the package trusts a signing key
explanation: The package ships a signing key into a keyring folder, or its script imports one, so packages signed with that key install without a warning.
remediation: Check the key belongs to the vendor, and that the apt source using it is scoped with signed-by.

title: The package installs a program with raised privileges
explanation: A file in the package is setuid or setgid, so it runs with its owner's rights, usually root's, whoever starts it. Browsers' sandbox helpers are a common, expected case.
remediation: Check the package is meant to need it.

title: The package installs files that run at boot or login
explanation: The package ships services, timers, cron jobs, autostart entries, login scripts, loader configuration, PAM, sudo or udev rules. These take effect without anything being opened.
remediation: Check each one is expected for this package.

title: The package puts files in home or temporary folders
explanation: The package installs into /home, /root, /tmp, /var/tmp or /dev/shm. Package managers install into system folders; these paths are outside what they track and remove.
remediation: Do not install it unless the vendor explains why.

title: A PKGBUILD download is not checked against a checksum
explanation: A source that is not a version-control checkout or a signature file has SKIP for its checksum, so makepkg builds with whatever the server returns.
remediation: Ask the maintainer for a real checksum, or check the file yourself before building.

title: The AppImage is not signed
explanation: The AppImage has no embedded signature. Most do not, so this is common; it means only the download's origin vouches for it.
remediation: Download it from the project's own site and compare its checksum with the one published there.

title: The AppImage can update itself
explanation: The AppImage carries update information, so an update tool can replace it with whatever that address serves.
remediation: Check the address belongs to the project.

title: This is a program launcher, not a document
explanation: A .desktop file runs the command on its Exec line when opened. It can sit in a folder or an archive looking like any other file. Commands it runs are also checked with the installer rules.
remediation: Open it only if you expected a program from where it came from.

title: A program launcher is made to look like a file
explanation: A .desktop launcher borrows a document's look: a double extension like report.pdf.desktop, a Name such as Invoice.pdf, or a PDF, office or folder icon. File managers show the Name and icon, so it reads as a document while opening it runs a command.
remediation: Do not open it. Delete it unless you know who made it and why.

title: A program launcher downloads something when opened
explanation: The launcher's command runs curl or wget. What it downloads is not part of this check and can change at any time.
remediation: Do not open it.

title: A decoy file was opened or changed
explanation: A canary decoy was read, changed, moved or removed while the monitor was running. inotify cannot say which program did it.
remediation: Check what was running at that time. Backups, indexers and your own tests can also trigger decoys.

title: Local read detection verified
explanation: A deliberate read of the decoy produced a fresh receipt from the running monitor, so local detection works.
remediation: Leave monitoring running.

title: Desktop pop-ups are not available
explanation: notify-send is not installed, so canary alerts appear in Activity but not as pop-ups.
remediation: Install your distribution's desktop notification utilities if you want pop-ups.

title: Listens on every network interface
explanation: A program accepts connections on all of this computer's network addresses, so other machines on the same network can reach it.
remediation: If only this computer uses it, make it listen on 127.0.0.1, or stop it.

title: The container API is open on the network
explanation: Docker's API is listening on TCP. Whoever reaches it can start containers with root access to this machine.
remediation: Use the local socket instead, or require TLS client certificates.

title: A remote debugger is reachable from the network
explanation: A debugger port (Node.js inspector, Chromium DevTools, debugpy) is open beyond this computer. Debuggers let whoever connects run code in the program.
remediation: Bind the debugger to 127.0.0.1, or stop it when you are done.

title: A local AI or notebook server is reachable from the network
explanation: A server that usually has no login (Ollama, Jupyter, Gradio and similar) listens beyond this computer.
remediation: If only you use it, bind it to 127.0.0.1.

title: SELinux stopped or logged an access
explanation: SELinux refused a program something its policy does not allow, or logged it when the program runs in a permissive domain. This is the system's own defense working.
remediation: If the program needed this to work, a local policy module can allow it; Bigman shows the record and never changes policy for you.

title: AppArmor stopped or logged an access
explanation: AppArmor refused a confined program something its profile does not allow, or logged it in complain mode.
remediation: If the program needed this to work, its profile can be extended; Bigman shows the record and never changes profiles for you.

title: The SSH server is on
explanation: sshd accepts logins from other computers. On a desktop it is often turned on once and forgotten, and it is the way in that the October 2026 tampered editor extension used through a reverse tunnel. Review when other computers can reach it or no firewall is running, Info when the firewall blocks it or you logged in over the network recently.
remediation: If you do not log in to this computer remotely, turn it off; the undo turns it back on. Bigman will not turn it off while you are logged in over the network.

title: cups-browsed adds printers from the network
explanation: cups-browsed listens for printer announcements from the whole network. Its 2024 vulnerabilities (CVE-2024-47176 and related) let a device on the network add a printer that runs commands when you print. Review when other computers can reach UDP 631.
remediation: Turn it off unless you rely on network printers appearing by themselves; printers already set up keep working.

title: A network service a desktop rarely needs is on
explanation: rpcbind, Samba, an FTP or telnet server, xrdp or Cockpit is enabled. Each accepts connections from other computers. Review when the firewall lets other computers reach it, Info otherwise.
remediation: Turn off the ones you do not use; the undo turns each back on.

title: No firewall is running
explanation: Neither firewalld nor ufw is active, so any program that listens on the network is reachable from every network this computer joins. Review when something is listening, Info when nothing is yet.
remediation: Turn on the firewall your distribution ships; Bigman can do it for firewalld or ufw.

title: The firewall opens every high port
explanation: A firewalld zone on an active network allows a wide range of ports, like Fedora Workstation's 1025-65535, so development servers, debuggers and anything else listening on a high port are reachable. Review when a program is reachable only because of the range, Info otherwise.
remediation: Close the range and allow the few ports you need by name.

title: Programs can read each other's memory
explanation: kernel.yama.ptrace_scope is 0, so any program running as you can attach to your other programs and read secrets out of their memory.
remediation: Set it to 1: programs can still debug what they start, and sudo is needed to attach to anything else.

title: Kernel addresses are visible to programs
explanation: kernel.kptr_restrict is 0, so kernel memory addresses are shown to every program, which helps local kernel exploits.
remediation: Set it to 1; profilers then need sudo for kernel symbols.

title: Every program can read the kernel log
explanation: kernel.dmesg_restrict is 0. The kernel log can reveal addresses and hardware details useful to an exploit.
remediation: Set it to 1; dmesg then needs sudo.

title: This computer asks the local network for names
explanation: systemd-resolved uses LLMNR, so names missing from DNS are asked of every device on the local network, and any of them can answer. On public Wi-Fi that is used to capture sign-ins and redirect connections.
remediation: Turn LLMNR off with a resolved drop-in; .local names and DNS keep working.

title: The screen does not lock by itself
explanation: GNOME or KDE Plasma is set never to lock when you step away, or not to lock after sleep.
remediation: Turn automatic locking on; Bigman sets a five-minute delay that you can change in your desktop's settings.

title: Someone is logged in automatically at startup
explanation: The display manager logs an account in without a password when the computer starts. Review when the disk is also unencrypted, Info otherwise.
remediation: Turn automatic login off in your desktop's user or login-screen settings.

title: The disk is not encrypted
explanation: The system or home folder is not on an encrypted device, so anyone holding the disk can read your files and keys.
remediation: Encryption is set up when installing; back up and reinstall with encryption on.

title: Secure Boot is off
explanation: The firmware starts any boot loader and kernel, so boot-level malware can load before Linux.
remediation: Turn it on in the firmware setup, after enrolling the signing key of any out-of-tree kernel module you use.

title: Your account is in the docker group
explanation: Members of the docker group can start a container that mounts the whole disk, which is administrator access without a password, for you and for any program you run.
remediation: Leave the group and use sudo, rootless Docker or Podman; the undo adds you back.

title: Other accounts can open your home folder
explanation: Your home folder lets other accounts on this computer list or open it. Review when other people's accounts exist, Info otherwise.
remediation: Remove access for others (chmod o-rwx); the undo restores the previous mode.

title: npm runs dependency install scripts
explanation: npm runs preinstall, install and postinstall scripts from every dependency during npm install. Self-spreading npm worms in 2025 ran from those scripts.
remediation: Set ignore-scripts=true in your user .npmrc and rebuild only the packages that need it.

title: Lynis recommendation
explanation: Lynis reported a warning or suggestion. The line is shown exactly as Lynis wrote it.
remediation: Look up the Lynis test ID before changing configuration.

title: A dependency has a published advisory
explanation: OSV lists a known vulnerability for a version this project depends on. A vulnerability is not evidence of malware.
remediation: Read the advisory's affected and fixed versions and update the dependency.

title: YARA-X rules matched
explanation: Rules you supplied matched the target. A match is the result of those rules, not proof of malware.
remediation: Check where the rules came from and what they look for.
